rationale: Distinguishing granulomatous from non-granulomatous iridocyclitis is a classic OP examination trap — mutton-fat KPs are pathognomonic of granulomatous disease and indicate specific systemic aetiologies.
Cycloplegic mydriatics are used in iridocyclitis to prevent posterior synechiae AND relieve ciliary spasm — both goals must be understood, as this is a common exam question on rationale of treatment.
Seclusio pupillae leading to iris bombé is the classic structural complication of iridocyclitis — understanding its mechanism (aqueous outflow block) prevents confusion with open-angle glaucoma.
Systemic immunosuppressants are second-line in uveitis management — understanding the correct therapeutic ladder prevents incorrect escalation or omission steps in exam scenarios.
Distinguishing hyphema from hypopyon by physical characteristics is a core clinical skill — the colour and behaviour of the collection are the key discriminators tested in MBBS examinations.
Rebleed in hyphema (secondary haemorrhage at day 3-5) is the most dangerous complication and is a classic exam focus — the timing and mechanism must be known.

HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis is the highest-yield systemic association in OP examinations — knowing the linked conditions (AS, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, IBD) and the clinical pattern is essential.

Toxoplasma gondii is the most common cause of posterior uveitis worldwide — this is a high-frequency exam fact that candidates often confuse with the most common cause of ALL uveitis (anterior uveitis, which is HLA-B27-related).
